title: India Considers Tripling FDI Approval Threshold to ₹15,000 Crore, Easing Path for Large Foreign Investments
excerpt: The CCEA's current ₹5,000 crore ceiling — unchanged since 2015 — would give way to faster ministry-level clearances for deals up to $1.8 billion
body:
• India is considering tripling the CCEA's FDI approval threshold from ₹5,000 crore to ₹15,000 crore, a limit unchanged since November 2015
  • The move would let line ministries clear larger foreign investments without Cabinet-level review, cutting bureaucratic delays for deals up to roughly $1.8 billion
  • A parallel proposal would exempt downstream foreign investments from fresh government approval where the upstream Indian entity already holds clearance
  • India attracted a record $94.5 billion in gross FDI in FY26, with cumulative inflows crossing $1.16 trillion since 2000

A Decade-Old Ceiling Under Review

The Indian government is weighing a proposal to raise the threshold at which foreign direct investment proposals require approval from the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) — from ₹5,000 crore to ₹15,000 crore, according to sources familiar with the discussions reported by PTI.

https://x.com/CNBCTV18News/status/2089617209371062649

The CCEA is a high-level body chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, with members including the Home Minister and Finance Minister. Under India's current FDI policy, any proposal involving total foreign equity inflow above ₹5,000 crore must be placed before the CCEA for approval. Below that limit, the relevant line ministry decides on its own.

That ₹5,000 crore ceiling has remained unchanged since November 2015. Government sources told PTI that prevailing economic conditions, inflation, and the growing scale of global investments now necessitate an update. A committee of secretaries has already recommended the upward revision in an earlier meeting.

"Prevailing economic conditions, inflation, the growing scale of investments over the years, and the objective of promoting ease of doing business necessitate a review of the existing threshold."

— Government sources, via PTI

What Changes for Foreign Investors

If adopted, the reform would mean that FDI proposals worth up to ₹15,000 crore — roughly $1.8 billion — could be cleared at the ministry level without waiting for Cabinet committee review. For context, the CCEA previously raised this floor from ₹1,200 crore to ₹3,000 crore in 2015 under the Make in India push, then bumped it to ₹5,000 crore months later.

The practical impact is faster approvals. Large investments in sectors that require the government approval route — defence, media, telecommunications, multi-brand retail, and others — have historically faced delays at the CCEA stage. A higher threshold would shift a significant volume of proposals to streamlined ministry-level processing.

The proposal is still at a discussion stage, sources said, with no timeline announced for a formal decision.

Downstream Investment Rules Could Also Ease

Alongside the threshold change, the government is separately considering a relaxation of rules governing downstream or indirect foreign investment. Under the proposal, fresh government approval would be waived for indirect foreign investment in an Indian company where the upstream domestic entity has already received clearance.

Currently, prior government approval is required for downstream investments in two situations: sectors under the government approval route for FDI, and investments originating from countries sharing a land border with India — a restriction introduced in April 2020 to prevent opportunistic takeovers during the pandemic. Recent Press Note 2 of 2026 has already begun loosening some of those border-country restrictions, though the formal notification under FEMA is still being processed by the Department of Economic Affairs.

Record FDI Year Sets the Stage

The proposed reforms come as India posts its strongest FDI numbers yet. Gross FDI inflows hit $94.5 billion in FY2025-26, up roughly 17% year-on-year and the fastest growth in six years, according to DPIIT data. FDI equity inflows reached a record $58.85 billion, an 18% jump from $50.02 billion in FY2024-25.

Cumulative FDI into India since April 2000 has now crossed $1.16 trillion. The top source countries remain Singapore (24.7%), Mauritius (23.7%), and the United States (10.4%). Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Gujarat together account for roughly two-thirds of all state-level inflows.

Why NRI Investors and Diaspora Businesses Should Watch

For Non-Resident Indians and diaspora-led businesses exploring investments back in India, the proposed changes carry direct implications. A higher CCEA threshold means mid-sized NRI-backed ventures — joint ventures in real estate, infrastructure, food processing, or tech services — could clear government approval faster and with less uncertainty.

The downstream investment easing is equally relevant. NRI investors who hold stakes through intermediate Indian holding companies currently face a second layer of government approval for any reinvestment into sectors on the approval route. Removing that requirement would simplify capital deployment and reduce compliance costs for diaspora investors structuring multi-tier investments.

Combined with India's broader push to streamline FDI rules and recent FTA negotiations, the reforms signal a clear effort to reduce friction for large-scale foreign capital at a time when global investors are actively diversifying supply chains away from China.
nri_angle: A higher CCEA threshold and eased downstream investment rules mean faster approvals and simpler capital deployment for NRI investors and diaspora-led businesses structuring investments in India, particularly in sectors requiring the government approval route.
